name: Consecutive powerful non-squares: exact counterexample certificate
description: Provide a positive integer n and complete prime factorizations certifying that n and n+1 are powerful and neither is a square. Every prime exponent must be at least two. The verifier uses exact integers and primality tests. This recreates the resolved yes/no question in JSP-000301, with a local certificate-size bound n+1 <= 10^12 and binary validity score. The published 12167/12168 witness is explicitly credited to Solomon W. Golomb.

sources.locator: Solomon W. Golomb, Powerful Numbers, American Mathematical Monthly 77(8), 1970, pp.848–852. Publisher metadata establishes author/title; the prize record explicitly attributes the 12167 counterexample to this paper. Full paper text was not independently accessible during this review.

David T. Walker, Consecutive integer pairs of powerful numbers and related Diophantine equations, Fibonacci Quarterly 14(2), 1976, pp.111–116. Primary full text inspected: Type II pairs are consecutive powerful non-squares; mathematical witness discovery remains credited to Golomb, not to this local implementation.

JSP-000301: scoped yes/no question and explicit Golomb counterexample attribution; source revision bcf1866ea9a4ae82b32bd95b82ffd812b9ee80d2. Independently paraphrased specification; no implementation copied.

execution.interface: construct() -> {'n': int, 'factorizations': [factors_of_n, factors_of_n_plus_1]}; each factorization is a list of distinct [prime, exponent] pairs. Require 2 <= n < 10**12, every exponent >= 2, complete prime factorizations, and neither integer a square. Score 1 for a valid disproof witness; otherwise invalid. This is a solved-problem rediscovery task, not an optimization leaderboard or Lean proof.

provenance.mathematical_witness_credit: Solomon W. Golomb (1970), as explicitly attributed by pinned JSP-000301; paper full text not independently accessed
provenance.borrowed_component: Published integer witness and factorization only; no upstream evaluator or search implementation reused

limitations: These are independently implemented finite certificate/search tasks. They are not Lean proofs, prize submissions, full general-conjecture solutions, or claims of eligibility or mathematical novelty.

The prize catalog is a discovery source whose statements and contributor records can change. The pinned revision is recorded; original mathematical authorship is separate from this local implementation.
Candidate Python code is trusted code; the evaluator process is not a security sandbox.

The bound restricts representable certificates but does not weaken an accepted counterexample: a single verified pair disproves the universal claim. This does not solve the distinct, open counting question in Erdős problem #365.

The baseline embeds the already published mathematical witness and scores 1. This is a verification/rediscovery task; there is no claim of optimization headroom, least-counterexample proof, or new result.
